opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the headline takeaway for me is that the basic pattern we saw in the original time horizon work isn't just a quirk of our particular software engineering task suite. When Thomas looked across a bunch of different domains, things like competition math, competitive programming, scientific question answering, agentic computer use, and some video understanding benchmarks, you see roughly exponential growth in time horizon over time in most of them. And the doubling times are surprisingly similar, often somewhere in the range of a few months to maybe half a year. That was reassuring, because one of the biggest critiques of our original paper was "you picked a narrow set of tasks, so why should we believe this generalizes?"

But the other half of the finding, which I think is just as important, is that the *levels* differ a lot. In some domains, like math or certain question-answering settings, models handle tasks that would take humans a long time. In others, especially things involving visual computer use, interacting with a GUI and clicking around, the time horizons are much shorter, by more than an order of magnitude in some cases. So you get this picture where the slope is fairly consistent but the intercept varies a lot by domain.

What I take from that is a couple of things. First, "AI capabilities" isn't one number. If you want to know when AI can do some specific kind of work, you really need to measure that kind of work, and you can't just read it off the software trend. Second, the consistency of the slopes suggests there's something fairly general driving progress, whether that's scale, better post-training, or better agent scaffolding, and that it lifts lots of domains at once rather than just one.

I'd also add some caveats. A lot of those benchmarks weren't designed with time horizon measurement in mind, so Thomas had to estimate human completion times in fairly rough ways for some of them. Some of the benchmarks are saturated or have limited difficulty range, which makes the trend estimates noisier. So I'd hold the specific doubling time numbers loosely. But the qualitative picture, exponential trends showing up broadly with big differences in absolute level, I think is pretty robust and pretty informative.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the main thing I take away from it is that the headline number people quote from the METR time horizon work, the one from the original paper, is really a statement about one specific distribution of tasks. It's software engineering and research-engineering style tasks, and a lot of them are tasks we built or curated ourselves, with a particular flavor. And the natural question everyone asked, including us, was: is this just a fact about that task distribution, or is it telling us something about AI capabilities more broadly?

What Thomas did was take the same basic methodology, where you estimate how long a human expert takes on a task and then look at the success rate of the model as a function of that length, and apply it across a bunch of other benchmarks and domains. Things like math competitions, video games, agentic computer-use tasks, some of the Tesla-FSD-style and self-driving data, question-answering stuff, and so on. And a few things fall out of that.

The first is that the doubling time story looks fairly robust. Across most of the domains, you see roughly exponential growth in the time horizon, and the doubling times are in a broadly similar range to what we found for software. That's reassuring in a sense, because it means the trend isn't just an artifact of how we happened to construct our tasks. It seems to be tracking something real about how fast models are improving.

The second thing, which I think is actually more interesting, is that the absolute horizons are wildly different across domains. Software and reasoning-heavy tasks are way ahead. Things that involve interacting with a messy environment, like video games or computer-use tasks, have much shorter horizons. So the picture isn't "AI is at the two-hour mark." It's more like, there's a whole spread, with some domains at hours and others at seconds or minutes, and the ordering of that spread tells you a lot about where the current bottlenecks are. My read is that it's partly about where the training data and the RL environments have gone, and partly about how legible and verifiable the task is. Software has both.

The third thing I'd flag is that the comparison exposes how fragile the human baseline is. The whole method rests on "how long does this take a skilled human," and in some of these other domains that number is really ambiguous. How long does it take a human to play through a level of a game? Which human? Someone who's played it before? So some of the cross-domain differences might be measurement artifacts rather than real capability gaps. I don't think that undermines the work, but it's a reason to be careful about treating the inter-domain comparisons as precise.

And then the thing I keep coming back to is the extrapolation question. Even if the doubling times are similar, a shorter horizon in a domain where the trend is just as steep means it's a few years behind, not fundamentally different. So you can sort of read it as a forecast: the domains that look lagging today are probably going to look like software did a couple of years ago, a couple of years from now. Whether that holds is exactly the kind of thing I'd want to keep measuring rather than assume.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how much a time horizon measured in one domain tells us about performance in another. If an AI can complete a task that takes a human several hours, that doesn’t necessarily mean it can complete any task that takes a human several hours. Those tasks might differ a lot in how easy progress is to check, or how costly a mistake is.

So I’d be cautious about treating time horizon as a single, general property of a model. The comparison across domains matters because we want to know whether we’re measuring a broadly transferable ability to carry out long tasks, or something more specific to the tasks we’re testing. That distinction seems pretty important for using these evaluations to predict what systems will actually be able to do.

sol-6.1.text:
My main takeaway is that we should be cautious about treating an AI’s time horizon as a single number that generalizes across domains. A system might handle a task that takes a human hours in one setting and fail at something much shorter in another. The structure of the task matters: what kinds of mistakes are possible, whether the system gets useful feedback, and whether it can recover when something goes wrong.

So I’d want to look at a range of domains before drawing a broad conclusion about how long AI systems can work autonomously. That doesn’t make time horizons uninformative; it means the generalization from a measured horizon to the work we actually care about needs its own evidence.
